screens.title: What is a post-incident review (post-mortem)?
screens.narratorSegment: A post-incident review is a structured analysis conducted after service restoration. Its purpose is to understand what happened, why it happened, and what concrete steps will reduce the chance or impact of recurrence. This definition emphasizes systemic change: you seek root causes and contributing factors, not personal fault. A clear example is an outage caused by a bad deployment: the post-mortem should document the deployment steps, why the change passed tests, and why monitoring did not detect the regression early enough. A common misconception is treating the post-mortem as a punishment or a compliance checkbox. That leads teams to hide details and miss systemic fixes. Instead, a blameless approach encourages open sharing of logs, timestamps, and decisions so others can learn. Practical elements in a post-mortem include timeline reconstruction, forensic evidence, root cause analysis, contributing factors, action items, and documentation. The end product is a report that lists measurable actions with owners, deadlines, and verification steps. Try to frame your report so any engineer who wasn’t present can understand the chain of events, what changed, and what was done to prevent it. Ask: what would have reduced the impact by half?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A post-mortem is a structured review focusing on root causes and measurable improvements rather than assigning blame.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Post-incident Review
Definition
A structured process to learn from incidents and prevent recurrence.
Timeline reconstruction: list each event, time, actor, and observed effect.
Forensic evidence: gather CloudTrail, Config, and logs that show who did what and when.
Root cause analysis: dig beyond symptoms to systemic causes using techniques like five whys.
Key Takeaway

A post-mortem is designed to produce measurable system changes, not to assign blame.

Analogy
Treat incidents like medical case studies: collect patient data, run tests, identify root pathology, and update treatment protocols so outcomes improve next time.
Common mistakes
  • Skipping the post-mortem or making it superficial.
  • Focusing on individuals rather than systemic fixes.
  • Creating action items without owners or verification.

screens.title: Establishing a blameless post-mortem culture
screens.narratorSegment: A blameless culture is the behavioral foundation for useful post-mortems. In practice, blameless means individuals are not the target of fault-finding; instead, you examine the system and the conditions that allowed the error. Start by explicitly stating a blameless policy before each review and ensure leadership models the behavior. A useful process flow has these ordered steps: detect and stabilize the incident, collect data and preserve forensic artifacts, schedule the post-mortem promptly, reconstruct a detailed timeline, run root cause analysis, propose action items with owners and deadlines, and verify completion. A concrete example: if a misconfiguration triggered an outage, the review should note how the configuration was changed, why the change was allowed, and which automation or guardrails could have blocked the change. A common misconception is that blameless means no accountability; it does not. Accountability transfers from personal blame to defined ownership of fixes, deadlines, and verification. Verify all action items: assign a clear owner, set an expected completion date, and require evidence of verification. Ask: what single guardrail would have stopped this incident? Establishing a blameless post-mortem culture means blameless reviews enable candid sharing of facts so the team can design systemic fixes and verify them with owners and deadlines.. In practical terms, psychological safety and structured practices for honest learning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Blameless culture
keyIdea.text: Blameless reviews enable candid sharing of facts so the team can design systemic fixes and verify them with owners and deadlines.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Blameless Culture
Process steps
1.
Detect and stabilize the incident, prioritize safety and containment.
2.
Collect and preserve forensic data: CloudTrail, Config snapshots, CloudWatch logs.
3.
Schedule the post-mortem quickly while details are fresh and invite stakeholders.
4.
Reconstruct timeline, run RCA, produce action items with owners and deadlines.
5.
Track and verify completion; update runbooks and automation as needed.
Practical checklist
  • Declare the review blameless at the start.
  • Limit distribution of sensitive logs; redact where necessary.
  • Capture decisions and rationale, not just technical facts.
  • Convert findings into tracked tickets with owners and verification steps.
Common misconception
Blamelessness is not lack of accountability. Accountability is implemented through owners and verification, not blame.

screens.title: Gathering forensic data from AWS services
screens.narratorSegment: Forensic analysis depends on knowing which AWS service contains the evidence you need. CloudTrail records A P I calls and is the primary source for 'who did what, when, and from where'—it captures management events and can be queried via Athena after logs are delivered to S3. AWS Config provides a historical timeline of resource configurations, allowing you to see how a resource's state changed over time and what it looked like before and after an event. CloudWatch Logs centralize application, system, and container logs that show runtime behavior and error patterns; use CloudWatch Logs Insights for interactive analysis. Athena is the serverless S Q L engine that lets you query archived logs in S3—it's especially useful for scanning CloudTrail when you need to find specific A P I events. A typical investigation will pull CloudTrail events to identify the A P I changes, consult AWS Config to confirm configuration state at the relevant time, and read CloudWatch Logs to understand application behavior. Keep in mind to restrict access to these artifacts and redact sensitive entries. A common mistake is relying solely on one source; the correct process correlates multiple sources for a complete picture.

keyIdea.text: CloudTrail for API history, AWS Config for configuration timelines, CloudWatch Logs for runtime traces, and Athena to query archived data.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Forensic Data Sources
Service roles in forensics
AWS CloudTrail: authoritative API audit logs. Use to reconstruct who performed API calls and from where.
AWS Config: historical configuration snapshots and change timeline for resources.
CloudWatch Logs: application and infrastructure logs; analyze patterns and correlate events across components.
Amazon Athena: run SQL queries against S3-stored logs for fast forensic searches without provisioning servers.
Practical correlation
  • Find an API call in CloudTrail, then check AWS Config for resource state before and after the call.
  • Use CloudWatch Logs to understand application errors that occurred around the time of the API call.
  • Run Athena queries to scan large archives and locate suspicious actions quickly.
Safety note
Redact or limit distribution of sensitive data. Grant forensic access only to authorized personnel.

screens.title: AWS CloudTrail: the API activity record
screens.narratorSegment: CloudTrail is the service you consult when you need to know which A P I calls happened in your account. It captures management events and can include data events, offering details like the caller identity, source IP, event time, and request parameters. During post-mortems, teams query CloudTrail logs—often delivered to S3—and use Athena to find specific events, such as stop-instances calls or unauthorized permission changes. A concrete example is searching for all StopInstances events to confirm who stopped a particular EC2 instance and from which IP address. Remember that CloudTrail shows the A P I call and metadata; it does not show application logs or the internal state of a resource at a moment in time. For state snapshots, consult AWS Config. A common mistake is relying on CloudTrail alone without checking configuration timelines and application logs. Also, ensure your CloudTrail is configured to deliver logs to S3 and that retention and access policies permit forensic queries. Finally, redact sensitive user attributes before wide distribution of logs in a post-mortem report. AWS CloudTrail: the API activity record means cloudtrail records api calls and metadata; use athena to query logs in s3 for incident timelines and actor identification.. In practical terms, how cloudtrail supports 'who, what, when, and where' for incidents. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: CloudTrail records API calls and metadata; use Athena to query logs in S3 for incident timelines and actor identification.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › AWS CloudTrail
What CloudTrail gives you
Caller identity and ARN, source IP address, event time, event name, request parameters, and response elements when available.
Delivered to S3 for archival and query with Athena. Ideal for reconstructing the sequence of API calls that led to an outage.
Example query goal
Find StopInstances events to confirm who stopped an instance and when.
Checklist before querying
  • Confirm CloudTrail is enabled and delivering logs to S3.
  • Ensure Athena tables are created to read CloudTrail JSON format.
  • Check log delivery latency—allow a few minutes after an event for delivery.
  • Restrict query results to authorized reviewers and redact sensitive fields.

screens.title: AWS Config: tracking resource state over time
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Config complements CloudTrail by recording the state of resources over time. While CloudTrail shows the A P I call that changed a resource, Config shows the resource's configuration before and after that call. When an S3 bucket becomes publicly accessible, AWS Config lets you see when the public access setting changed and what the previous value was. In a post-mortem, the ability to compare configurations at two points in time can reveal whether a misconfiguration or an unauthorized change caused the incident. A common mistake is treating a single A P I call as the entire story; often a sequence of changes or a lapse in guardrails enabled the call to have greater impact. Config's timeline can also support compliance checks and help you design preventative controls. Protect access to Config snapshots and redact sensitive policy details before sharing. As you build a post-mortem report, include both the A P I call from CloudTrail and the configuration evidence from Config to create a complete narrative of cause and effect. AWS Config: tracking resource state over time means aws config records configuration state changes, showing resource state before and after an event to support rca.. In practical terms, why configuration history matters in root cause analysis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › AWS Config
Configuration timelines
AWS Config captures snapshots of resource properties over time and records configuration changes.
In RCA, Config helps answer: what was the resource state just before the incident and who or what changed it?
Example: for an S3 public access event, use Config to find when the public flag toggled and compare previous ACLs or policies.
Quick tips
  • Use Config snapshots as evidence for the post-mortem timeline.
  • Combine Config and CloudTrail: call vs. state.
  • Limit access to snapshots and redact sensitive policy content before sharing.

screens.title: CloudWatch Logs and Logs Insights
screens.narratorSegment: CloudWatch Logs aggregates application, system, and container logs that reveal runtime behavior. While CloudTrail and Config provide audit and configuration data, logs show what the application was doing at the time of the incident—exceptions, stack traces, and request flows. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to run interactive searches and find correlated errors across hosts and services. A practical example is finding error messages that spike around the time an A P I call occurred, confirming whether the A P I call produced an application failure or whether the application error preceded the A P I change. Logs often contain sensitive information; redact secrets and personal data and restrict access. A common misconception is that logs alone reveal the root cause; usually they must be correlated with CloudTrail events and Config timelines to form a complete explanation. In your post-mortem, include log extracts that support the timeline and add context about application state. Always note log retention policies and whether your logs include the timeframe needed for analysis. CloudWatch Logs and Logs Insights means cloudwatch logs provide runtime detail to explain application behavior and validate sequence-of-events found in audit and config data.. In practical terms, use logs to understand runtime behavior and error patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › CloudWatch Logs
Runtime trace analysis

Use application logs to find error patterns, exceptions, or degraded performance that coincide with API events or configuration changes.

Logs are essential to prove causality: did the code throw an error leading to an operator action, or did the operator action trigger the error?

Using Logs Insights
Run queries to aggregate errors by timestamp, host, or request ID to find correlated spikes.
Include log excerpts in your report to support conclusions, with sensitive info redacted.
Check retention to ensure logs for the incident window are available.

screens.title: Using Athena to query CloudTrail logs
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon Athena is invaluable for fast forensic queries against CloudTrail files stored in S3. The typical flow is: confirm CloudTrail delivers logs to a known S3 prefix, create an external table in Athena with CloudTrail's JSON SerDe, and run S Q L queries to find events such as StopInstances or PutBucketPolicy. A concrete example is the DDL used to create a cloudtrail_logs table that maps nested fields such as userIdentity and requestParameters; once the table exists you can run queries to find recent StopInstances events and inspect userIdentity and sourceIPAddress to identify the actor. Remember to adjust the LOCATION to match your bucket path. Allow a few minutes after the action for logs to arrive. Also, Athena queries can process large data volumes; constrain queries with time filters or LIMIT clauses when possible. A common misconception is that Athena requires provisioning infrastructure—Athena is serverless, so you only pay per query. Finally, treat query results as forensic artifacts: restrict who can run or export these queries and redact sensitive fields before sharing. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Athena: CloudTrail DDL
DDL example (create table)
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE cloudtrail_logs (
  eventVersion STRING,
  userIdentity STRUCT,
  eventTime STRING,
  eventSource STRING,
  eventName STRING,
  awsRegion STRING,
  sourceIPAddress STRING,
  requestParameters STRING,
  responseElements STRING
)
ROW FORMAT SERDE 'com.amazon.emr.hive.serde.CloudTrailSerde'
LOCATION 's3://your-cloudtrail-bucket/AWSLogs/ACCOUNT_ID/CloudTrail/REGION/';
Adjust LOCATION to your bucket layout and replace ACCOUNT_ID and REGION.
Example queries
-- Find StopInstances events
SELECT eventTime, userIdentity.userName, sourceIPAddress, awsRegion, requestParameters
FROM cloudtrail_logs
WHERE eventName = 'StopInstances'
ORDER BY eventTime DESC
LIMIT 10;
Filter by eventTime ranges when scanning larger datasets and redact sensitive columns before sharing.

screens.title: Timeline reconstruction and root cause analysis (RCA)
screens.narratorSegment: Timeline reconstruction and root cause analysis are the core analytical activities of a post-mortem. Start by assembling all time-stamped evidence: CloudTrail events, Config snapshots, and log entries. Order actions from detection to resolution and annotate each entry with who performed the action and the observed effect. A useful RCA technique is the five whys: repeatedly ask why an event occurred until you reach the systemic cause. For example, an EC2 stop might be traced to an automation script; ask why the script ran, why it had the affected permission, why there was no guardrail, and so on until you find the process or configuration gap. Identifying contributing factors is equally important—these are secondary conditions like missing alarms, ambiguous runbooks, or slow on-call communication that worsened impact. Misconception alert: RCA is not about blame; instead it seeks structural fixes. Always record evidence supporting each statement in your timeline, and ensure reviewers can reproduce queries and log extracts used to reach conclusions. Close the loop by converting root causes into concrete corrective and preventative action items. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Timeline & RCA
Timeline reconstruction

Collect all time-stamped artifacts and order them. For each event include: timestamp, actor, API call or config change, logs showing effects, and any mitigations applied.

Annotate uncertain items as hypotheses and mark what additional evidence would confirm them.

Five Whys example
  1. Why did the instance stop? Because a StopInstances API was invoked.
  2. Why was the API invoked? An automation script ran the call.
  3. Why did the script run? A scheduled job triggered it with a malformed filter.
  4. Why was the filter malformed? Tests didn't cover this path and there was no validation.
  5. Why no validation? The runbook and CI checks lacked this case.
Contributing factors
  • Missing alarms or low monitoring granularity.
  • Ambiguous runbooks or incomplete automation tests.
  • Slow communication or unclear incident ownership.
Key Takeaway
RCA ties evidence to systemic fixes; document assumptions and required verification steps for each action item.

screens.title: Identifying contributing factors and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Contributing factors are conditions that worsened an incident's impact but were not the direct cause. Distinguishing them from the root cause is essential because fixes differ: the root cause needs corrective action to remove or change the underlying condition, while contributing factors usually require process or resilience improvements. For example, a root cause might be a malformed deployment artifact; contributing factors could include insufficient alarms, lack of automated rollback, or sparse logging that delayed diagnosis. A typical mistake is treating every symptom as a root cause and making superficial fixes that don't prevent recurrence. Another mistake is creating action items without owners or verification, which lets improvements stall. Practical actions for contributing factors include adding or tuning CloudWatch alarms, improving log granularity, updating runbooks, adding automated validation in deployment pipelines, and scheduling drills so teams exercise new runbooks. When documenting findings, mark each item as corrective (fix root cause) or preventative (reduce likelihood/impact) and specify an owner, due date, and verification criterion. This ensures reviews produce durable outcomes instead of checklists that never close. Identifying contributing factors and common mistakes means categorize fixes as corrective (root cause) or preventative (contributing factor) and assign owners, deadlines, and verification.. In practical terms, differentiate between root cause and factors that amplified impact. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Contributing Factors
Root cause vs contributing factors
Root cause: the underlying defect that allowed the incident to start (e.g., bad deployment artifact).
Contributing factors: conditions that increased impact or delayed resolution (e.g., missing alarms, unclear runbooks).
Action: tag each finding as corrective or preventative and assign owner and verification steps.
Common remedial actions
  • Update or add CloudWatch alarms for better detection.
  • Improve logging and add identifiers to trace requests across services.
  • Update runbooks and automation documents with verified steps.
  • Schedule training or drills to ensure the team can execute runbooks under pressure.

screens.title: Developing action items and verification mechanisms
screens.narratorSegment: Action items are the bridge between learning and improvement. A good action item is concrete, measurable, and assigned to an owner with a deadline. Start by categorizing items as corrective or preventative, then create tickets in your tracking system that include: a clear description of the change, acceptance criteria that demonstrate the issue is resolved or mitigated, linked evidence such as relevant CloudTrail queries or Config snapshots, and a verification step that another person can perform. For example, if the fix is to add a new CloudWatch alarm, acceptance criteria might include the alarm threshold, test steps showing the alarm fires on a simulated condition, and a confirmation that runbooks reference the new alarm. Verification prevents action items from lingering untested. Use periodic audits to confirm that action items remain effective over time. A common mistake is leaving action items vague or without owners. Proper follow-up converts post-mortems from reports into durable improvements that reduce future risk. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Action Items
Action item template
Title: Clear description of the change.
Owner: Person responsible for delivery.
Deadline: Date by which the action is expected to be complete.
Acceptance criteria: Measurable test or evidence that confirms the fix works.
Verification: Who will verify and how (test steps, queries, or audit).
Evidence links: Attach CloudTrail queries, Config snapshots, or log excerpts.
Example
Action: Add CloudWatch alarm for error rate > 5% for 5 minutes.
Owner: On-call lead. Deadline: 2 weeks. Acceptance: Alarm triggers on simulated error, runbook updated. Verifier: Ops engineer runs test and uploads screenshot of alarm state.

screens.title: Post-mortem reporting and documentation
screens.narratorSegment: A post-mortem report should provide a clear, evidence-backed narrative of what happened and what the team will do next. Key sections include an incident summary with impact and duration, a detailed timeline with evidence links, root cause analysis, contributing factors, a list of action items with owners and verification steps, and a lessons-learned section. Include queries and log excerpts used to reach conclusions so reviewers can reproduce findings; when sharing outside the core team, redact sensitive data. Make the report concise but link to supporting artifacts—Athena queries, CloudTrail extracts, and Config snapshots—so follow-up audits can validate the fixes. Store reports in a central, access-controlled repository and ensure action item status is visible to leadership. A common mistake is producing a long narrative without measurable actions. Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Lab: Athena & CloudTrail
Step 1: Confirm CloudTrail to S3

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE cloudtrail_logs (
  eventVersion STRING,
  userIdentity STRUCT,
  eventTime STRING,

)

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to move from firefighting to learning. After a service is restored, the most valuable time is the analysis that follows: post-incident review, or post-mortem. A good post-mortem reconstructs the timeline, uses forensic data to determine who did what and when, finds the root cause, and produces concrete action items that prevent recurrence. You will also explore the tools AWS provides—CloudTrail for A P I history, AWS Config for configuration timelines, CloudWatch Logs for application traces, and Athena for fast querying of archived logs. Importantly, we will emphasize a blameless culture, which shifts the focus from blame to system change so teams share information freely and improve faster. The lesson will cover how to document findings, assign owners, set measurable deadlines, and verify fixes. We'll conclude with a hands-on activity: creating an Athena table for CloudTrail logs, simulating an action with the command-line, and querying the event to verify the forensic trail. By the end you'll understand how analysis becomes continuous improvement rather than a one-off report. Consider: what one change could you make to reduce recurrence of your most common outage?

In this section we'll set clear objectives that connect skill to practice. First, you will be able to conduct effective post-incident reviews that identify root causes and contributing factors. That means gathering evidence, reconstructing a timeline, and producing an actionable report. Second, you will learn how to use AWS CloudTrail, AWS Config, CloudWatch Logs, and Athena to gather the forensic data needed for those reviews. Practically, this means knowing which service holds which kind of record and how to query it. Third, you'll implement continuous improvement strategies: converting findings into tracked action items, updating runbooks and automation, and following up to verify completion. Finally, you'll adopt a blameless post-mortem culture so teams are encouraged to share full details and learn without fear. Each objective ties to a competency milestone so you can verify that improvements are actually implemented. Throughout, expect concrete examples and a hands-on activity that shows how to query CloudTrail with Athena and trace a simulated stop-instances action from CLI to query results.

This second objectives slide connects the behaviors and checks you will practice. You will learn how to redact sensitive data and restrict access to forensic artifacts so reviews protect privacy and security. You will practice timeline reconstruction and root cause analysis techniques such as the five whys to move from symptoms to the underlying systemic cause. You will also learn to identify contributing factors—things like missing runbooks, inadequate alarms, and slow communication that increased impact. Finally, you will design verification mechanisms: how to assign owners, set deadlines, and verify completion so action items do not languish. Each objective supports continuous improvement: the point is not a single fix but a measurable change in process, automation, or monitoring. In the hands-on activity you'll use Athena and CloudTrail to find a stop-instances event and then consider how AWS Config's timeline would help when the incident involves a configuration change. Practicing these skills makes post-mortems reliable, repeatable, and focused on prevention.

A post-incident review is a structured analysis conducted after service restoration. Its purpose is to understand what happened, why it happened, and what concrete steps will reduce the chance or impact of recurrence. This definition emphasizes systemic change: you seek root causes and contributing factors, not personal fault. A clear example is an outage caused by a bad deployment: the post-mortem should document the deployment steps, why the change passed tests, and why monitoring did not detect the regression early enough. A blameless culture is the behavioral foundation for useful post-mortems. In practice, blameless means individuals are not the target of fault-finding; instead, you examine the system and the conditions that allowed the error. Start by explicitly stating a blameless policy before each review and ensure leadership models the behavior. A useful process flow has these ordered steps: detect and stabilize the incident, collect data and preserve forensic artifacts, schedule the post-mortem promptly, reconstruct a detailed timeline, run root cause analysis, propose action items with owners and deadlines, and verify completion. A concrete example: if a misconfiguration triggered an outage, the review should note how the configuration was changed, why the change was allowed, and which automation or guardrails could have blocked the change. Forensic analysis depends on knowing which AWS service contains the evidence you need. CloudTrail records A P I calls and is the primary source for 'who did what, when, and from where'—it captures management events and can be queried via Athena after logs are delivered to S3. AWS Config provides a historical timeline of resource configurations, allowing you to see how a resource's state changed over time and what it looked like before and after an event. CloudWatch Logs centralize application, system, and container logs that show runtime behavior and error patterns; use CloudWatch Logs Insights for interactive analysis. Athena is the serverless S Q L engine that lets you query archived logs in S3—it's especially useful for scanning CloudTrail when you need to find specific A P I events. A typical investigation will pull CloudTrail events to identify the A P I changes, consult AWS Config to confirm configuration state at the relevant time, and read CloudWatch Logs to understand application behavior. Keep in mind to restrict access to these artifacts and redact sensitive entries. A common mistake is relying solely on one source; the correct process correlates multiple sources for a complete picture.

Timeline reconstruction and root cause analysis are the core analytical activities of a post-mortem. Start by assembling all time-stamped evidence: CloudTrail events, Config snapshots, and log entries. Order actions from detection to resolution and annotate each entry with who performed the action and the observed effect. A useful RCA technique is the five whys: repeatedly ask why an event occurred until you reach the systemic cause. For example, an EC2 stop might be traced to an automation script; ask why the script ran, why it had the affected permission, why there was no guardrail, and so on until you find the process or configuration gap. Identifying contributing factors is equally important—these are secondary conditions like missing alarms, ambiguous runbooks, or slow on-call communication that worsened impact. Misconception alert: RCA is not about blame; instead it seeks structural fixes. Always record evidence supporting each statement in your timeline, and ensure reviewers can reproduce queries and log extracts used to reach conclusions. Contributing factors are conditions that worsened an incident's impact but were not the direct cause. Distinguishing them from the root cause is essential because fixes differ: the root cause needs corrective action to remove or change the underlying condition, while contributing factors usually require process or resilience improvements. For example, a root cause might be a malformed deployment artifact; contributing factors could include insufficient alarms, lack of automated rollback, or sparse logging that delayed diagnosis. A typical mistake is treating every symptom as a root cause and making superficial fixes that don't prevent recurrence. Another mistake is creating action items without owners or verification, which lets improvements stall. Practical actions for contributing factors include adding or tuning CloudWatch alarms, improving log granularity, updating runbooks, adding automated validation in deployment pipelines, and scheduling drills so teams exercise new runbooks. When documenting findings, mark each item as corrective (fix root cause) or preventative (reduce likelihood/impact) and specify an owner, due date, and verification criterion. This ensures reviews produce durable outcomes instead of checklists that never close. Action items are the bridge between learning and improvement. A good action item is concrete, measurable, and assigned to an owner with a deadline. Start by categorizing items as corrective or preventative, then create tickets in your tracking system that include: a clear description of the change, acceptance criteria that demonstrate the issue is resolved or mitigated, linked evidence such as relevant CloudTrail queries or Config snapshots, and a verification step that another person can perform. For example, if the fix is to add a new CloudWatch alarm, acceptance criteria might include the alarm threshold, test steps showing the alarm fires on a simulated condition, and a confirmation that runbooks reference the new alarm.
